Strongest pairwise correlations in a data frame

Source: R/profile_extra.R
topcors.Rd

Ranks the numeric column pairs by the strength of their association and returns the strongest, so a wide table's structure can be read without squinting at a correlation matrix. Use it on a new data set to find near-duplicate columns, derived columns and the relationships worth a closer look.

Usage

topcors(data, n = 10L, meth = c("spearman", "pearson"), minabs = 0)

Arguments

data

A data frame; non-numeric columns are ignored.

n

Number of pairs to return, one positive whole number (default 10).

meth

"spearman" (default) or "pearson".

minabs

Report only pairs whose absolute correlation reaches this, a number in \([0, 1]\) (default 0).

Value

A data frame of class c("bricklayer_correlations", "data.frame") with x and y (character, column names), correlation (numeric) and abscor (numeric), strongest first, at most n rows; the method is in attr(, "method"). The print method draws a signed bar per pair.

Details

Spearman is the default deliberately. Pearson measures LINEAR association only, so it understates a relationship that is perfectly monotone but curved, and a single outlier can manufacture or destroy it. On data you have not yet inspected – which is the situation this function is for – the rank correlation is the safer question to ask.

Non-numeric columns are ignored. Each pair uses the rows where both values are present; a pair with fewer than three such rows, or with a constant column, has no correlation and is left out. Pairs are ranked by absolute correlation, those below minabs dropped, and the first n returned. cortbl() gives every pair, with the number of rows behind each. A progress bar is drawn on stderr for many pairs unless options(morie.quiet = TRUE).

Errors: data not a data frame; fewer than two numeric columns; n not one positive whole number; minabs not one number in \([0, 1]\); an invalid meth.

See also

cspr(), ccovm(), cortbl()

Examples

set.seed(1)
n <- 200
df <- data.frame(
  a = stats::rnorm(n),
  b = stats::rnorm(n),
  grade = sample(letters[1:3], n, TRUE)
)
df$c <- df$a * 2 + stats::rnorm(n, sd = 0.1) # strongly related to a
df$d <- exp(df$a) # monotone but curved

topcors(df)
#> ── Top correlations (spearman) ─────────────────────────────────── 
#>  x y correlation                  plot
#>  a d       1.000           |##########
#>  a c       0.998           |##########
#>  c d       0.998           |##########
#>  a b      -0.062          #|          
#>  b d      -0.062          #|          
#>  b c      -0.060          #|          
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 

# The curved pair is ranked correctly by Spearman and understated by
# Pearson, which is why Spearman is the default.
tc <- topcors(df, meth = "spearman")
tc[tc$x == "a" & tc$y == "d", "correlation"]
#> [1] 1
tp <- topcors(df, meth = "pearson")
tp[tp$x == "a" & tp$y == "d", "correlation"]
#> [1] 0.8496382

# Filter to the pairs worth looking at, and keep the top two.
topcors(df, n = 2, minabs = 0.5)
#> ── Top correlations (spearman) ─────────────────────────────────── 
#>  x y correlation                  plot
#>  a d       1.000           |##########
#>  a c       0.998           |##########
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 

# a threshold above 1 is an error
try(topcors(df, minabs = 2))
#> Error : `minabs` must be a single value in [0, 1]
